cells.tense: You're at the table with the pen, and both the weighing and the call are happening right now.
cells.ask: Take the next real decision that lands on you today — not the big one you've been saving — and say your call out loud in one sentence. It hands you back the sound of your own voice deciding.
cells.core:
You can hold a thing in your mind long enough to hear what's true about it, then set it down and move. That's the whole trick, and you have it. People get a direction from you that doesn't wobble — not because you rushed, but because you didn't. That's a rare thing to be around, and you're not making a production of it.

The pause is doing its job right now. It hasn't turned into hiding and it hasn't turned into pushing. What's in front of you is more of the same: something worth seeing clearly, then a move. You've stopped being shy about the move. The next real thing to decide is probably already sitting there, and saying it aloud is the whole of it.
cells.sheetLine: You weigh it, then you move, and both halves are yours.
cells.verb: weighing what you know before you commit to a direction
cells.place: in the part of your life where you decide what to do next

cells.tense: You're already at a decision that hasn't happened yet, rehearsing how it'll go.
cells.ask: Take something you've been circling and do the smallest visible version of it before you feel ready — send the message, book the slot, say the sentence. The doing tells you whether the circling was worth it.
cells.core:
Weighing is supposed to end. Yours has gotten very good at not ending — another angle, another comparison, one more thing to check before it's safe to commit. Two truths are still being held and the grip has stopped believing it's allowed to drop one. That grip is costing you, and it's costing the people waiting on a direction from you.

Running as it should, this is simpler than it sounds: you take in what you know, you don't need the outcome in advance, and you move. The picture you're bracing against is a future you're writing wholesale, and no amount of preparation arrives pre-approved. The move you're avoiding is smaller than the version in your head. Do that one today, before you've finished deciding it's the right one.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already open, still deciding whether to go through.
cells.ask: Tell one person a direction you've actually chosen — not the reasoning, just the direction — and let it land without defending it. It pulls current back through the place that's gone quiet.
cells.core:
You're leaning one way and not saying so. Undecided in public, decided underneath, which is how a person ends up following whichever thing was loudest that week. What you can see clearly is there, and it isn't being spent.

In good shape this doesn't look like much. You say what you already see, you don't argue for it, and the people around you stop guessing where you stand. Naming one thing is enough to get the current moving — not by trying harder at deciding, but by giving the direction somewhere to go. The thing you're already leaning toward is the one to name.
cells.sheetLine: You've leaned one way and you're standing still.

cells.tense: The pen is down and you're still writing, and you'd say the page is writing itself.
cells.ask: Name one thing you decided this week and say, simply, that you decided it. It puts the pen back in the hand that's been holding it.
cells.core:
The steering is happening. Direction has your fingerprints on it, the calls get made, and things go somewhere. With this in good order, you're the one picking, without a fuss, and the people around you can feel that the ground is settled.

The claim hasn't caught up. The talking about it treats the direction as something that arrived on its own, so the picking goes unnamed and the credit drifts off. The next time someone asks why you're doing what you're doing, tell them you picked it. Not the whole case. Just that it was you. That's the whole ask, and it takes about four seconds.
